idiom_name: immutable amount + unit value type with one conversion table or registry
implementation_notes: Language-neutral structure: make one immutable type whose two components are the amount and the unit, construct it only through a validating factory, and give it the four behaviours that must not live at call sites - unit-compatible addition and subtraction with one documented conversion policy, comparison, conversion to another compatible unit (delegated to a conversion-ratio object or a registry when the unit set is large), and amount-plus-unit parsing/formatting. Keep every conversion factor in exactly one table keyed by unit identity, and make incompatible operations fail loudly: compile-time where the type system allows, otherwise an explicit error rather than a coerced number. Multiplication and division by scalars is the minimum contract; quantity-by-quantity multiplication that yields a compound unit is the richer option and requires a unit algebra (dimension exponents), which is what type-level implementations provide for free. Model absolute affine units such as temperatures separately from their differentials, or arithmetic will produce physically meaningless values.
code_sketch:
value Quantity
  amount: Number                 # the numeric part, in this quantity's unit
  unit: Unit                     # atomic, or compound as a product of powers
  create(amount, unit)           # validate + normalise, reject invalid
  +, -, compare(other)           # convert to a compatible unit, else error
  as(unit): Quantity             # delegate to Conversion Ratio / registry
  parse(text): Quantity          # '3 km' -> amount 3, unit km
# conversion factors live in one table/registry, never at call sites
pitfalls: Carrying the unit outside the type - in a variable name, a parallel variable or an int code - so every call site has to remember it; that is exactly the bug the pattern removes.

Choosing the conversion policy by accident: silent conversion hides precision and rounding decisions, while refusing all mixed-unit arithmetic pushes the work back to callers - decide and document one policy.
Leaving the value mutable so a quantity can be rescaled in place while other code still holds a reference to it.

Wrong move: pass a bare number through an integration boundary and rely on a documented unit convention -> a producer/consumer mismatch can silently corrupt calculations, as the Mars Climate Orbiter loss showed -> instead serialize the amount and unit together and validate or normalize on ingress.

Wrong move: apply ordinary addition or multiplication to absolute Celsius/Fahrenheit values -> affine offsets make the result physically meaningless despite looking numerically valid -> instead distinguish absolute points from temperature differences and restrict operations.

Wrong move: duplicate conversion factors in each feature or service -> rounding and definition drift make equal quantities disagree across boundaries -> instead centralize factors in one versioned registry and test conversions against authoritative unit definitions.
